questions.question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Retrieve
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Recover**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Synonym means identical or almost identical in meaning to another word or phrase in the same language.
 
• The word '**Retrieve'**( verb) means to bring or get something back.
 
 
• *Example- The program allows you to **retrieve** data within a few seconds.*
 
• ​*Example- She bent to **retrieve** her glasses from the floor.*
 
 
 
• Similarly, the word '**Recover' **(verb) means to get something back or to get back to the previous situation or position.
 
 
• *Example- (From illness)- Rita is still **recovering** from her operation.*
 
• *Example- (From something unpleasant)- The economic condition of the country is beginning to **recover**.*
 
• Example- (Something stolen or lost)- *The police **recovered** the stolen money from the thieves.*​
 
 

Therefore, the appropriate synonym for **Retrieve** is **Recover**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The word **'Remove'**( verb) means to take something or somebody away from a place or to get rid of something unpleasant.

 
 
• *Example- John **removed** his hands from her shoulder.*
 
• *Example*- *She **removed** her glasses and looked at the thing.*
 
• *Example- It was difficult to **remove** the stain from the curtain.*
 
 
 
• The word '**Rescue**' (verb) means to save something or somebody from a dangerous situation.
 
 
• ​*Example- She **rescued** a man from drowning.*
 
 
 
• 'Rescue' as a noun means the act of saving something or somebody from a difficult situation.
 
 
• ​​*Example- A policeman came to their **rescue** when they were attacked by robbers.*
 
 
 
• **Retain' (**verb)** **means to keep something or to continue to have something.

 ​*Example- He managed to **retain **control of the situation.*

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

Millions of people / have been protected / from polio by a fluid / called as a vaccine.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **called as a vaccine**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The fourth part of the sentence contains a grammatical error.
 
• The correct form would be **called a vaccine**.
 
• **'called as a vaccine'** is not appropriate for this particular sentence because here the sentence implies that millions of people are protected from polio by a fluid **which is called a vaccine**. 
 
• The name of the particular fluid is vaccine so we can say that the fluid is **called a vaccine**.
 
• Writing '**called a vaccine'** solves the purpose of the sentence and the meaning of the sentence can easily be understood.
 
• **'Called'** here is a verb form that can be used instead of '**named'** or '**known as'**.
 
• It can be used with '**as'** when the meaning shows '**was selected to be'. **
 
 
• *Example- He was **called as** a manager in the year 2001*.
 
 
 
• **'Called as'** can be used in a sentence when it refers to somebody who has called you over the telephone.
 
 
• *Example- I just **called you up as** a wellwisher, not as a teacher*.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Game is up

options.text: Game is over and winner declared

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Deception is at an end**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **'Game is up'** means to let someone know that you are aware of their hidden plans or activities and that they must stop.

 
 
• *Example- Okay, the **game is up**, we know that you have stolen the gold chain.*
 
• *Example- John, the **game is up**! The cops discovered your fingerprints all over the door.*
 
 
 
• Hence, the appropriate meaning is '**Deception is at an end'** because when someone's '**game is up'**, they can no longer get away with doing something dishonest or unlawful because they've been caught.

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• An **idiom** is a set of words whose meaning has been established by usage as distinct from that of the individual terms.
 
• The ancient Greek term '**idioma**' meant '**peculiar phraseology**', the English word "**idiom**" came from this.
 
• **Idioms** exist in every language.
 
• **These** are often used by people who speak or write to get their point across in a more creative way.
 
• Some common examples of **idioms**:
 
 
• ***Once in a blue moon** means **rarely***. 
 
• *Example- You come to our house **once in a blue moon**.*
 
• ***Sell like hot cakes** means **quick sellout and in large quantities.***
 
• *Example- Her books are **selling like hot cakes**.​*

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.

Do you mind / whether I use / your telephone?
questions.solution:
The correct answe is **whether I use. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Here instead of '**whether'** we should use the word '**if'** because it is sounding more appropriate.
 
• In indirect yes-no questions and questions with or, we apply whether.
 
 
• *Example- He wants to find out **whether** the rooms have a heater **or** not.*
 
 
 
• When we are just asking and not talking about options or alternatives we can use '**if'**.
 
 
• *Example- Would you mind **if** I ask you to sit?*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **If** and **whether** are frequently interchangeable, yet they have different applications.
 
• **If** and **whether** are subordinating conjunctions.
 
• When describing a possible selection of actions, **whether** is preferred over **if**; **if** is better saved for the introduction of a condition.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.

The actor along with his new wife __is expected__ shortly.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **No substitution required**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When two subjects are linked by words like '**along with**', '**together with**', '**as well as**', etc., the verb agrees with the first subject. Therefore, we use **is** or **was,** or **has** instead of **are**, **were,** or **have**.

 
 
• *Example- The director **along with** his wife **has** come to our house.*
 
• Example- He **as well as** his daughter **sings** well. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• This is known as subject-verb-agreement of a sentence where the **subjects and verbs agree with each other in terms of number** (singular or plural).
 
• If the subject of a sentence is **singular** the verb of that sentence should also be **singular**.
 
• If the subject of a sentence is plural the verb of that sentence should also be plural.
 
• There are many subject-verb-agreement rules in English Grammar.

questions.question:

Reading not only helps to pass the leisure hours __as well as__ keeps you well informed.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Usually, **not only...but also** works as a **pair** like "either-or" and "neither nor".
 
• These conjunctions are used **to connect words or phrases** of the same grade.
 
 
• **Example:** *I have **not only** completed my homework **but also** the assignments. *
 
 
 
• **As well as** is used to **add some new information to the given information** and mostly the verb following as well as will be in its "-ing" form. 
 
 
• **Example**: *Rita sings **as well as** composing music. *
 
 
 
• Therefore, but also is the appropriate replacement. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Along with** - used to show accompaniment.

 
 
• **Example**: *A gift came **along with** this letter.*
 
 
 
• **And even** - used to show importance or emphasis with the tone of surprise.
 
 
• **Example:** *Jenny went to Dubai with her friends **and even** did Skydiving.*

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

The cat / drank the milk / before we / return home.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**return home**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the **action has already happened**. That is, the cat has already drunk the milk.
 
• It is in the **past tense.** 
 
 
• **Example:** *Jim **sang** well at the concert. *
 
 
 
• So, **"return**" should also be in the **past tense**. But, it is given in the **present tense** in the sentence.
 
• Therefore, the sentence should have been, "The cat drank the milk before we **returned home**."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Past tense** can be divided into **four types.**
 
• **Simple Past Tense - ***Tim **walked** to the market.*
 
• **Past Continuous Tense - ***Tim **was walking** to the market.*
 
• **Past Perfect Tense - ***Tim **had walked** to the market.*
 
• **Past Perfect Continuous Tense - ***Tim **had been walking** to the market.*

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no.5.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**invaluable**". [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Let us understand the meaning of the correct word:
 
• **Invaluable**: Something that is invaluable has **unimaginable value**. It's inestimable.
 
 
• Example: *This watch was a gift from my grandfather, so it is invaluable.*
 
 
 
• As we can see, the word "lesson" is a noun and it requires an adjective to modify it. Thus, "invaluable" is the perfect adjective that can enhance it.
 
 
• Example: *Even though they are difficult, these obstacles teach us invaluable lessons including how to gracefully tolerate uncertainty, impatience, and disarray.*
 
 
 
• From the above explanation, we can decipher that ‘**invaluable**' fits the best for the given sentence. As the lessons given by **nature** are **priceless**.
 
• Hence, the complete sentence is: *Most of all, spend time in the company of nature to pick up some invaluable lessons.​*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__***

Let us understand the meaning of the remaining words:

 
• Inevitable: that cannot be avoided or prevented from happening.

 
 
• Example: *Losing jobs was something that was inevitable.*
 
 
 
• Invisible: that cannot be seen; not perceptible by eyes.
 
 
• Example: *To the bare eye, the majority of microorganisms are invisible.*
 
 
 
• Innumerable: too many to be counted.
 
 
• Example: *Innumerable issues have caused frequent delays to the program.*

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Drag one’s feet

options.text: Do something deliberately at a slow pace
Find it difficult to walk fast
Be hurt badly on the foot
Have a disability in the feet

questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**do something deliberately at a slow pace**". [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

Let us understand the meaning of the given idiom:

__
 
• The idiom "**drag one’s feet**" means to walk slowly and wearily or with difficulty or be **deliberately** slow or **reluctant** to act.
 
• It refers to starting anything slowly or **refraining** from doing something you do not wish to do.
 
• This idiom typically refers to someone who is prepared to go cautiously and **hesitantly** because they do **not **want to accomplish something.
 
 
• **Example**: *Stop dragging your feet and hop into the car; we have to be on time for the doctor's appointment.*
 
 
 
• As the word, '**drag**' itself portrays 'to pull somebody/something along with difficulty' so the idiom is consequently associated with this meaning.
 
• Therefore, the correct meaning of the given idiom is: *Do something deliberately at a slow pace.​*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__***

 
• **Sluggish** is the word used for someone who finds it **difficult** to walk.
 
• **Wounded** is the word used for someone who is** hurt** badly.
 
• **Limping** is the word used for someone who has a **disability** in the feet.
